## Conclusion

The claim is **conditionally true**: opening a bedroom window or door tends to lower CO2 buildup and improve subjective/objective sleep quality, *but only when outdoor conditions (temperature, noise, air pollution) are favorable*. The mechanism is well-supported, though real-world benefits depend heavily on climate and location.

**Supporting evidence:** A controlled study by Eindhoven University of Technology (17 healthy young adults) found that leaving a window/door open reduced bedroom CO2 concentrations and was associated with better subjective and actigraphy-measured sleep quality plus improved next-day cognitive performance (research.aalto.fi study, reported by medicalxpress.com: https://medicalxpress.com/news/2017-11-windows-doors.html). Related Technical University of Denmark (DTU) research similarly concluded that ventilating a bedroom to keep CO2 below ~750–1,000 ppm preserves sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance (https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day).

**Important caveat:** A Shanghai field study of 41 households in summer found that opening windows improved air quality/CO2 levels but *worsened* overall sleep quality because open windows let in heat, noise, and PM2.5 pollution, which outweighed the CO2 benefit (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S036013232301051X). The Sleep Foundation's review of similar research echoes this trade-off (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed).

**Bottom line:** Ventilating the bedroom to reduce CO2 generally supports better sleep, but in hot, noisy, or polluted environments, opening a window can backfire. The benefit is context-dependent, not universal.
